Seems that two types of things are especially vulnerable to wall clipping glitches: Fine geometry and when there are physics involved.
How come that after all these years, game engines still have those wall clipping glitches?

Game engines only update so fast. At 60hz update rate if, you're travelling so fast that in 16 milliseconds you travel more than the width of a collision box, the game doesn't register a collision and you go through.
besides speed glitching, everyone right now is using common game engines like Unity, UE4, CryEngine, etc, and that helps us find their glitches in google.

The short answer is that objects in games do not track each and every pixel - that would be too expensive. Things are stuck in bounding regions - axis aligned bounding boxes, spheres, unaligned bounding boxes, planes, etc. And then collisions are determined between these regions. These tests are very high performance. For instance how do you detect if you have a collision between two spheres? So you simply take the distance between their central points. If that is less than the sum of their radii then they're colliding. You get a collision detection with something like a dozen floating point operations total. This is also why axis aligned bounding boxes are a much different beast than unaligned bounding boxes. Axis aligned bounding boxes are similar to spheres whereas unaligned bounding boxes require some work -- even if they're generally going to fit things much better than an axis aligned bounding box would. It's all about performance.

In some cases a collision can then be determined all the way down to a pixel perfect match (perhaps for hit detection from a small projectile) but that is a very expensive process. So for most cases the bounding regions are used suffice. There are many reasons that clipping can occur, but the most basic is when the actual drawing of a region ends up extending outside of its bounding region. Fine geometry is a good example. An exact pixel perfect collision test against fine geometry is very expensive, but it doesn't really provide that big of a difference versus really cheap bounding box collisions. So you use the bounding box and your left foot slightly clips through in the back, but your game runs 10x better than it would otherwise. 10x is an exaggeration, but the difference can really quite a bit higher than you'd intuit so in general it's a trade that's probably worth making.

If not for performance reasons (and on occasion lazy and/or incompetent developers) there'd be no clipping. Even the speed glitching people are mentioning can be worked against by verifying the path of an object between frames. But again, that comes with a price that in many cases cannot be afforded.
